b55acec11f:
Here are sixty scenario questions written to the CCDV-F blueprint (official guide v1.0, July 2026). The real exam has 53 items in 120 minutes, with a scaled pass mark of 720. This set runs a little longer so that every sub-objective gets covered, and the items are spread by domain weight.

As on the exam, questions are mixed across domains. Each one has a single best answer from four options.
26d402ab2a:
Work all 60 before you open any answer. Allow 135 minutes, which is the real pace of about 2.25 minutes per item.

Write your letters on the answer sheet, then mark them against the key. Read the rationale for every item you missed or guessed. Then fill in the domain-gap table to see which chapters to re-read.
0d8a2f2e97:
Most wrong options here are real features used in the wrong place:

  • a prompt instruction where a hook or code check belongs;
  • Batch where someone is waiting;
  • a bigger model where the context or data is the problem;
  • a retry for a deterministic 400;
  • a parameter the current models reject.

When two options both sound right, ask three things. Which one gives a guarantee? Which one addresses the root cause? And which one do the constraints in the stem actually require?
787def835c: Copy or print this grid and write your letter next to each number. Mark a question with ? if you guessed. A correct guess still counts as a gap.
164b374aed: The quick key comes first, for marking. Detailed rationales follow. Open each one only after you've committed to an answer.

6273962f30: Answer: C. Long-running work belongs behind an asynchronous contract. Accept the request, hand back a job ID, and let the client poll. That survives proxies and restarts.
90cbf92366: Answer: A. Descriptions and schemas are how the model learns to call a tool. An actionable error result lets it correct itself on the next turn.

6e8bfa5dc0: Answer: D. Larger tiers and higher effort help with reasoning depth. When the failure is missing information, the fix is to get that information into context.

45f4f8a372: Answer: C. On adaptive-thinking models, effort is the dial for how much thinking gets spent. The docs say tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models.
d9cf45319d: Answer: C. Bloat from tool output is the cause. Prune it at the source and clear results once they're used, so the window holds what the next decision needs.

b3e80a76b1:
The real exam reports a scaled score from 100 to 1000, with 720 to pass. The scaling isn't published, so a raw percentage here is only a proxy.

Treat about 75% (45 of 60) as the line to clear with some margin. Practice questions you've studied for are easier than unseen ones.
571bdfb693: When you look for gaps, count a correct answer you marked with ? as half right. A lucky guess on the exam is not a plan.
1b3015198f: For each domain, count your correct answers, divide by the number of items, and compare the result with the 75% target. The question numbers help you find the misses quickly.
b5c8b9a2a2:
Weighting matters when you choose what to study. A score of 50% in D2 costs you about a sixth of the whole exam. The same score in D4 costs under two percent.

So fix the large-weight gaps first. Then do the small domains. They're cheap to close, because each one is a single chapter.
0b40ffd691: Answer distribution in this set: A 15, B 15, C 15, D 15. Don't use letter frequency as a strategy.
